scams.name: The Gold Ring Trick
scams.description: You're strolling along the Seine near Pont des Arts when a woman ahead of you bends down and holds up a shiny gold ring. 'Excusez-moi, is this yours? I just found it — pure gold, look!' She presses the ring into your hand before you can respond, examines it theatrically, and declares it's too big for her. Then comes the pivot: a hard-luck story about her sick child, and wouldn't you know it, could you spare a few euros since you're so lucky to have found this valuable ring? The ring is brass stamped to look like 18K gold, worth pennies. Euro for Visitors reports the scam has been running continuously on Pont des Arts for over two decades.
scams.avoidance: Say 'Non, merci' firmly and keep walking without slowing down. Never touch or accept the ring — the moment you hold it, you're 'obligated' in their script. Ignore anyone who bends down dramatically in front of you near tourist sites. If they follow you, walk toward a group of people, a police officer, or a nearby shop.
scams.location: Pont des Arts, along the Seine near the Louvre, Champ de Mars, Tuileries Gardens

scams.name: The Sacré-Cœur Friendship Bracelet Trap
scams.description: You're climbing the famous white steps toward Sacré-Cœur in Montmartre when a man suddenly grabs your wrist with a warm 'From where? America? Welcome, friend!' In about 20 seconds he has woven a colorful string bracelet around your fingers and tied it tight before you've said a word. Then he's demanding €10, €20, sometimes €30, and his friends have quietly surrounded you. Travel and Tour World (2024) reported this scam targeting the 10.5 million annual visitors to Sacré-Cœur. In 2014, Paris Police Commissioner Bernard Boucault was slapped by bracelet scammers when he tried to intervene.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets as you climb the Sacré-Cœur steps. Say a firm 'NON!' and pull your arm back the instant someone reaches for your wrist. If cornered, loudly say 'Appelez la police!' — they scatter instantly. Visit Sacré-Cœur very early morning (before 8am) or take the Montmartre funicular instead of the steps.
scams.location: Steps leading to Sacré-Cœur Basilica, Montmartre hilltop, Place du Tertre approaches

scams.name: The Deaf-Mute Petition Pickpocket
scams.description: You've just stepped off the RER at Champ de Mars and a young woman approaches holding a clipboard. She points to her ears and mouth — deaf-mute — and gestures for you to sign her petition for 'disabled children.' The moment the pen is back in her hand, she flips to a donation page showing previous 'donors' who gave €10, €20, €50. If you refuse, her accomplices have already lifted your phone from your back pocket while you were focused on the clipboard. At CDG airport, petition scammers attacked Aéroport de Paris workers who warned tourists about them.
scams.avoidance: Never sign anything from a stranger on the street in Paris — legitimate charities do not operate this way. Shake your head firmly, say 'Non,' and walk without breaking stride. Keep your phone in a front zipped pocket, not a back pocket or loose bag. Real French deaf organizations do not solicit on the street.
scams.location: Eiffel Tower south entrance, Louvre pyramid courtyard, Champs-Élysées, Opéra Garnier steps

scams.name: The Metro Door-Close Pickpocket Crush
scams.description: The doors of the Métro were about to close at Châtelet–Les Halles when three teenagers suddenly forced their way into an already-packed car, pressing everyone together. Only at your stop did you reach for your phone and find your jacket pocket empty. A 2016 investigation found a single gang was responsible for two-thirds of all metro thefts, employing approximately 100 young girls recruited from Eastern Europe with daily theft quotas of €300-€1,000. Paris generates more pickpocket-related travel reviews than any other city worldwide — 283 thefts per million tourists.
scams.avoidance: Keep valuables in a front zipped pocket, money belt, or inside jacket pocket — never outer or back pockets. If a group rushes the doors right at closing, let them pass and wait for the next train. Be extra vigilant at Châtelet, Gare du Nord, Opéra, and on RER B from CDG Airport. Board train cars near the driver's compartment where CCTV coverage is better.
scams.location: Metro Line 1 (Louvre, Champs-Élysées), Line 4 (Châtelet, Gare du Nord), RER B (CDG Airport)

scams.name: The Fake Police Officer Wallet Check
scams.description: Two men in plain clothes flash what look like police badges near Pigalle and ask to see your passport — standard drug-check procedure, they say. Nervous about being stopped by French authorities, you hand it over. One 'officer' inspects your passport while the other asks to verify your wallet isn't carrying counterfeit bills. While you're focused on the document check, your wallet disappears or cash is palmed. Real Paris police in plain clothes rarely stop tourists for random passport checks without a uniformed officer present, and they will never ask to inspect your cash.
scams.avoidance: Ask to be taken to the nearest commissariat (police station) — real officers will comply; scammers won't. Request a uniformed officer be present before showing any document. Keep your passport in your hotel safe and carry a photocopy instead. Call 17 (French emergency police line) immediately if you feel unsafe.
scams.location: Pigalle, near Moulin Rouge, backstreets near Opéra, Gare du Nord exits

scams.name: The Tourist-Zone Restaurant Overcharge
scams.description: The menu outside the café near Notre-Dame showed a croque-monsieur for €8, and you sat down feeling pleased. But the bill came to €34 — a €5 'couvert' (cover charge), the small bottled water you didn't order was €7, and the menu you'd seen was the 'lunch menu' that ended at noon. In July 2025, Le Parisien conducted a sting operation sending two journalists to the same Eiffel Tower-area restaurants — one dressed as a Parisian local, one as an American tourist. The American was charged approximately 50% more across all restaurants tested. French law requires identical pricing regardless of language — charging tourists more is fraud.
scams.avoidance: Ask 'L'eau du robinet, s'il vous plaît' (tap water, please) — it's free and legally required. Clarify 'C'est offert?' (Is this free?) when bread or nibbles are brought. Walk 2-3 streets away from major monuments for better prices. Service charge (service compris) is legally included in all French restaurant prices.
scams.location: Restaurants within 500m of Eiffel Tower, Champs-Élysées side streets, Notre-Dame area, Montmartre

scams.name: The Trocadéro Three-Card Monte
scams.description: A folding card table appeared near Trocadéro with a small crowd gathered around a fast-talking man shuffling three cups with a ball. You watched someone in the crowd win €50 — easy money, right? You put down €20 and lost. The 'winner' was a shill working with the dealer, the cheering crowd were accomplices. In August 2025, a TikTok video of American tourist Nathalia Duques crying after losing 'so much money' to the Eiffel Tower three-card monte went viral with 11 million views. Commenters: 'Imagine being scammed by 3 cups in 2025.' The game is mathematically impossible to win — the operator removes the ball during the shuffle.
scams.avoidance: Never bet on street gambling — the game is mathematically and physically rigged; you cannot win. The 'winners' are part of the crew. Walk past without stopping or watching — even spectating marks you as a potential target. If you've lost money, walk away immediately — trying to 'win it back' will only cost more.
scams.location: Trocadéro plaza, Pont d'Iéna, Champ de Mars riverbanks, Montmartre steps

scams.name: The CDG Airport Unlicensed Taxi Ambush
scams.description: You land at CDG exhausted from a transatlantic flight. In the arrivals hall, a well-dressed man approaches: 'Taxi? I take you to Paris, good price.' You agree to €70. But the 'taxi' is an unmarked car, there's no meter, and when you arrive at your hotel the driver demands €200, claiming traffic, tolls, and 'airport fees.' One traveler documented being charged €200 for a trip that should cost €56. At Gare du Nord, unlicensed operators quote €120+ for rides that official taxis do for €15-20. The official fixed rate from CDG is €56 to Right Bank, €65 to Left Bank — no exceptions, no 'extras.'
scams.avoidance: Only take taxis from the official queue outside baggage claim — look for the illuminated 'TAXI PARISIEN' roof sign. Know the official fixed rates: CDG to Right Bank €56, CDG to Left Bank €65. Use the G7 app or Uber/Bolt for pre-priced, tracked rides. The RER B train from CDG to central Paris costs €11.80 and takes 35 minutes.
scams.location: Charles de Gaulle Airport arrivals hall, Orly Airport exits, Gare du Nord Eurostar exit

scams.name: The Gare du Nord Station Gauntlet
scams.description: You step off the Eurostar into Gare du Nord, Europe's busiest station, and immediately you're approached: someone offers to help with tickets, another wants to take your photo, a third bumps into you while pointing at a map. Gare du Nord is the most-reported theft location in Paris. One scam involves men with fake ID badges offering to help you buy metro tickets with their bank card, then demanding you pay €20+ in cash for a €2.15 ticket. Another uses the 'photo' request to position you in a dark corner while accomplices separate you from your luggage.
scams.avoidance: Buy tickets from official machines (they have English option) or the SNCF/RATP counter — never from helpful strangers. Keep rolling luggage handle in hand and bag straps across body at all times. Walk with purpose directly to the metro/RER entrance or taxi queue — don't stop in the main hall. Know your connection before arriving — check the RATP app.
scams.location: Gare du Nord main hall, Eurostar arrivals exit, metro/RER connection corridors

scams.name: The Phone Snatch at Metro Doors
scams.description: You're standing near the metro doors scrolling through Google Maps when the departure chime sounds. In the split second before the doors close, a hand reaches in, snatches your phone, and the thief is on the platform as the train pulls away. By the time you process what happened, you're halfway to the next station. This is the most common phone theft method in Paris — perfectly timed to the door-closing sequence. In 2025, a new variant emerged targeting tourists who wear phones on long lanyards around their neck, with thieves cutting the cord in crowded cars. Phone theft in the Métro is now the number one petty crime in Paris.
scams.avoidance: Never use your phone near metro doors — step away from the door area when checking maps. Keep your phone in a zipped front pocket, not in hand or dangling from a lanyard. If you must check your phone, turn your back to a wall so no one can approach from behind. Be extra vigilant when the door-closing chime sounds — this is prime snatch time.
scams.location: All Paris metro lines, especially at Châtelet, République, Gare de Lyon

scams.name: The ATM Distraction & Skim
scams.description: You're withdrawing cash from an ATM near the Champs-Élysées when someone taps your shoulder: 'Excuse me, you dropped this €20.' You turn, and in that moment your card is swapped for a similar one, or your PIN is observed by an accomplice, or skimming hardware records your card details. Some Paris ATMs, particularly private (non-bank) machines near tourist sites, have been found with skimming devices attached. A March 2025 DailyMail report found one in ten tourists to France (212,000 people over five years) admitted to being scammed, with ATM fraud a significant contributor.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours — these are monitored and maintained. Cover the keypad completely with your other hand when entering your PIN. Before inserting your card, wiggle the card slot and keypad — skimmers are often loosely attached. Avoid private/independent ATMs in tourist areas — stick to major French banks (BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, Société Générale).
scams.location: Standalone ATMs in tourist areas, non-bank ATMs near attractions

scams.name: The Rose Seller Restaurant Shakedown
scams.description: You're enjoying a romantic dinner at an outdoor terrace when someone approaches with a basket of roses. 'For your beautiful lady?' He places a rose in her hand or on the table before you can respond. Now he demands €10, €15, even €20 for a single flower that cost him centimes. If you refuse, he becomes loud and aggressive, creating a scene that embarrasses you in front of your date and the surrounding diners. Some victims report rose sellers returning repeatedly throughout the meal. The sellers know tourists will often pay just to end the confrontation.
scams.avoidance: Say 'Non merci' firmly before the rose is placed down — don't let them put it on the table. Do not touch the rose — once you've touched it, they'll claim you've 'accepted' it. Request restaurant staff intervene if the seller becomes aggressive. Indoor seating eliminates the issue entirely — sellers don't enter restaurants.
scams.location: Outdoor restaurant terraces in Le Marais, Latin Quarter, Montmartre, along the Seine

scams.name: The Fake Airbnb Phantom Listing
scams.description: You found the perfect Paris apartment — 2 bedrooms near the Marais for €100/night, beautiful photos, great reviews. The 'host' contacted you outside Airbnb, offering a 15% discount for direct bank transfer. You paid €700 for a week. When you arrived, the address didn't exist, the host's phone was disconnected, and Airbnb's support couldn't help because the transaction happened off-platform. During the 2024 Olympics, multiple tourists arrived in Paris to find their 'confirmed' rentals were fake listings, leaving them homeless. Airbnb removed 59,000 fake listings in response to the epidemic.
scams.avoidance: NEVER pay outside of Airbnb's platform — the only protection is their payment system. Verify the exact address exists using Google Street View before booking. Read reviews carefully — look for specific details about the apartment, not generic praise. Book with Superhosts who have long track records. From January 2025, all legitimate Paris Airbnbs must have registration numbers.
scams.location: Online (Airbnb lookalike sites, Facebook Marketplace, WhatsApp contacts)

scams.name: The 'Clumsy Jogger' Bump-and-Lift
scams.description: You're walking through the Tuileries when a jogger collides with you from behind — apologizing profusely, checking if you're okay, brushing off your jacket. By the time they've jogged away, your phone is gone from your pocket. The 'clumsy jogger' is a classic distraction technique: the physical contact masks the lift, and the apology buys time for an accomplice or for the jogger themselves to create distance. Variations include someone dropping items at your feet, 'accidentally' spilling coffee on you, or asking you to help with a heavy map while their partner works your pockets.
scams.avoidance: If bumped, immediately check your pockets and bag while keeping eyes on the person. Don't let strangers touch your clothing to 'clean' spills — step back and handle it yourself. Keep valuables in zipped front pockets, not back pockets or open bags. If something feels wrong, loudly say 'Non!' and create distance.
scams.location: Jardin des Tuileries, Luxembourg Gardens, Seine riverbanks, jogging paths near tourist areas
